questions.question: What does @Transactional guarantee for the database steps inside a method?
options: They run faster because of caching
They all commit together or all roll back together
They are never visible to other users
questions.explanation: A transaction is all or nothing, so either every step is saved or every step is undone.

questions.question: By default, which exception type makes Spring roll back a @Transactional method?
options: No exception, rollback must be called by hand
questions.explanation: Spring rolls back on RuntimeException and Error, and commits on checked exceptions unless rollbackFor is set.

questions.question: A wallet starts at 1000. A @Transactional method subtracts 100 and then throws a checked IOException, with no rollbackFor. What is the balance afterwards?
questions.explanation: Checked exceptions commit by default, so the subtraction of 100 is saved and the balance is 900.

questions.question: A @Transactional method catches the exception inside a try/catch, prints a message and returns normally. The earlier updates are still saved. Why?
options: Spring saw a normal return and committed
questions.explanation: The proxy only sees whether the method throws, so a swallowed exception looks like success and the work is committed.

questions.question: Method a() in a service calls this.b() where b() is annotated @Transactional. When a() is called from a controller, b() runs without a transaction. Why?
options: Spring only supports one transaction per class
The call inside the class skips the Spring proxy
The controller must be annotated too
questions.explanation: The annotation works through a proxy, and a call from inside the same object never goes through it.
